items.bodyEn: Ishibe, the 51st post town, lies in Ōmi Province, today's Konan in Shiga. It sat about nine ri, roughly 36 km, from Kyoto, a full day's walk, so travelers who left the capital at dawn spent their first night here. The saying 京立ち石部泊まり records that rhythm. Hiroshige's print skips the town for a teahouse at nearby Megawa village.
items.ja: {京立|きょうだ}ち{石部泊|いしべど}まり
items.kana: きょうだちいしべどまり
items.sourceNote: Saying 京立ち石部泊まり; Ōmi gazetteers on Ishibe-juku; Hiroshige, 'Ishibe' (目川ノ里)

items.bodyEn: Megawa village, between Kusatsu and Ishibe, was famous for 菜飯田楽: rice cooked with chopped greens, served with skewered tofu grilled under miso. Hiroshige painted its teahouse for his Ishibe print. The name dengaku comes from the medieval 田楽 dancers who performed on a single stilt; a block of tofu on one skewer looked just like them.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, 'Ishibe: Megawa Village' (目川ノ里); Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entry 田楽

items.bodyEn: ずくめ, まみれ and だらけ all mean full of, but they do not swap. ずくめ says something consists entirely of one thing and can be pleasant: 黒ずくめ, いいことずくめ. まみれ is for stuff smeared over a surface: 泥まみれ, 汗まみれ, 血まみれ, and by extension 借金まみれ. だらけ is for unwanted things scattered through: 間違いだらけ, 傷だらけ. Never いいことまみれ.

items.titleEn: たる: Two Old Words Fused
items.bodyEn: The たる of 堂々たる and 教師たるもの is the attributive form of たり, a classical copula that formed when と and あり fused: 'is as'. Its sibling なり came from に plus あり. The same と plus ある survives in modern として and 〜とした, which is why 堂々たる and 堂々とした mean the same thing.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (Shōgakukan), entry たり (助動詞): 格助詞「と」+「あり」
